To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
(1) the inverse of the covariance matrix is biased and (2) that the covariance matrix itself is singular for $p \geq n$, which is a consequence of the bias in the covariance matrix.
(i) the inverse of the covariance is not an unbiased estimator, and (ii) the covariance matrix is singular.

(1) the maximum-likelihood covariance matrix is biased, (2) the bias is proportional to the inverse of the number of data vectors, (3) the inverse of the covariance matrix is singular, (4) the marginalised likelihood function and its confidence regions are biased, and (5) the marginalised covariance matrix is singular
In summary, our research is concerned with

the problem of how to estimate the inverse covariance matrix of data vectors, given a set of independent data sets, and how to construct confidence regions in the parameter space of models that are fitted to these data sets.
the question of how to obtain reliable confidence regions for model parameters from observational data.
the question of how well we can determine the inverse covariance matrix of a data set.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the maximum-likelihood method, when applied to a set of independent data vectors, yields a biased log-likelihood function with a biased inverse covariance matrix, and that the size of confidence ellipses is underestimated.

, for the idealised Gaussian noise model, the maximum-likelihood approach to parameter inference in the case of statistically independent data vectors is unbiased only if $p<n$. In the opposite case, the maximum- likelihood estimator is biased, the bias being a function of the ratio $p/n$.
the maximum-likelihood approach should be used with great care.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
one has to be very careful in using the maximum-likelihood method to obtain confidence regions.
we have to be very careful when using the maximum likelihood method to fit models to data.

the maximum-likelihood estimators for the parameters and the covariance matrix are not consistent estimators for the case of Gaussian noise with statistically independent data vectors, and that the size of confidence ellipsoids is underestimated.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the inverse of a covariance matrix estimated from data is biased.
the standard approach to estimate model parameters and the inverse covariance matrix from observational data can lead to biased results.
the standard approach to estimating confidence regions is flawed.
